text: This lesson closes out the chapter on a genuinely reassuring note. Window functions are one of the MORE portable areas of modern SQL, not less — and that's worth understanding clearly before we move into procedural code next chapter, where the story flips completely.

Window functions were standardized in SQL colon 2003, and unlike a lot of SQL history, vendors actually implemented that standard closely. Row underscore number, over, partition by SalesPersonID, order by OrderDate descending. Rank. Dense rank. Same function names, same OVER clause, same PARTITION BY and ORDER BY syntax — on T-SQL, on Oracle, on MySQL 8-point-0 and later, and on PostgreSQL. The only thing that changes between those platforms in a query like this is identifier casing convention, not the syntax itself.

LAG and LEAD — reaching to a previous or following row within the same partition — and using an aggregate function like SUM as a window function instead of a GROUP BY aggregate are part of that same standard, and just as consistent. LAG of TotalDue over order by OrderDate gives you the previous order's total. SUM of TotalDue over order by OrderDate gives you a running total. A running total, a month-over-month comparison, a top-N-per-group query — all of this transfers directly from your T-SQL knowledge, with zero new concepts, on every platform in this course.

That said, there are two small, real places where platform differences still show up, so you're not caught off guard. First: when no explicit frame clause is given, the default frame an aggregate window function uses can behave subtly differently between platforms specifically when there are ties in the ORDER BY. Second: some of the more advanced frame syntax — named windows using the WINDOW keyword, which PostgreSQL and MySQL support but T-SQL doesn't, and newer frame-exclusion options — varies by platform. Neither of these affects the everyday usage you just saw; they only matter once you're writing unusually precise running-total logic.

Here's why this matters heading into what's next. The querying side of SQL — joins, CTEs, set operations, and now window functions — is largely one shared vocabulary across these four dialects, with only a handful of naming quirks along the way. Procedural SQL is a completely different story: stored procedures, control flow, error handling — none of that ever got fully standardized. That's exactly why T-SQL and PL/SQL are about to look dramatically different from each other, starting next chapter. Window functions are about as portable as this course gets — enjoy it while it lasts.

Next up: Chapter Five, Procedural SQL Overview — T-SQL versus PL/SQL versus stored programs on MySQL and PostgreSQL. This is where the real divergence in this course begins, so take a moment to appreciate how consistent everything in this chapter has been before we dive in.
